case_study_insert.main_stem: Westmoor Eco Panels (WEP) is a private limited company in the construction materials and recycled panel sector, employing a workforce of 31. Founded in 2015 by Rhys Westmoor, the business supplies composite wall panels to builders and operates a flat organisational structure with laissez-faire leadership. WEP plans to invest $690,000 in a recycled-composite panel line using agricultural waste fibre, financed by a $260,000 lease and $430,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $186,000 a year, a variable cost of $7.50 a unit and a selling price of $13.50, and produces 72,000 units of panel a year. WEP faces two problems: a shortage of trained machine operators and rising panel waste.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations and Waste Log — Q3 2025: The panel line produced 18,000 units last quarter at a defect rate of 2.2%, up from 1.4% a year ago. Waste fibre ran at 9.1% of input against a 6% target. Customer complaints rose from 22 to 35 per month. Average delivery to builders is 4.1 days. A survey of 520 building contractors found that 59% would pay up to $0.55 more for recycled-composite panels, and 51% check the environmental credentials of panel suppliers. A training audit shows 12 of 31 staff lack on-the-job training on the new pressing line; off-the-job courses at the college cost $820 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Westmoor Eco Panels for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.25% to 5.00%, raising the cost of the $260,000 lease. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.5% from $12.70 to $13.53 per hour from April 2026, raising total wage bills. (3) Recycled fibre, resin and transport input costs rose 12.1% year-on-year, while commercial building activity grew 2.2% over the same period.

questions.question_text: WEP plans to fund its recycled-composite panel line with retained profit rather than the $260,000 lease. Explain two advantages for WEP of using the $430,000 retained profit instead of the lease.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Using $430,000 of retained profit avoids the regular rental payments and finance charges attached to the $260,000 lease, protecting cash flow while WEP already carries fixed costs of $186,000 a year. The saving can be used to reduce the 2.2% defect rate and the 9.1% waste fibre level, or absorbed if recycled fibre, resin and transport costs keep rising 12.1%, allowing the $13.50 selling price to hold for builders.

Point 2: Retained profit leaves ownership of the new panel line with Rhys Westmoor and the company, so there is no risk of the leased equipment being repossessed if the shortage of trained machine operators delays commissioning or panel waste stays high. The lease would lock WEP into fixed payments irrespective of the 35 monthly complaints. Internal funds also keep the $690,000 investment free of lender conditions and preserve borrowing capacity for later expansion of the recycled-composite range.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to WEP's cash flow, waste and ownership.

questions.question_text: WEP is promoting its recycled-composite panels to building contractors. Consider advertising in a building trade magazine, sponsoring a construction exhibition, or a targeted social media campaign. Which should WEP choose? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Building trade magazine advertising: A trade magazine reaches contractors and can explain the agricultural waste fibre content and panel specifications, relevant to the 51% who check suppliers' environmental credentials. It is a credible medium that supports a $13.50 price. However, it is costly for a 31-employee company with a $260,000 lease, the readership is wider than WEP's builder base, and print cannot demonstrate the panels or react quickly to the 2.2% defect rate.

Construction exhibition sponsorship: A stand lets contractors see and handle the recycled-composite panels, ask about waste fibre and verify credentials face to face, directly addressing the 51% who check suppliers. It also supports the 59% who would pay $0.55 more by making quality visible. The drawbacks are the cost of a good stand, reach limited to attendees, and the fact that one exhibition cannot win orders for 72,000 units a year on its own.

Targeted social media campaign: Paid social ads can be aimed at regional builders and contractors, showing short videos of the pressing line and linking the $0.55 premium message to the environmental story. It is measurable, cheap per contact and quick to adjust if the 9.1% waste problem needs explaining. It depends on builders using the platforms and requires continued spend, and it reaches fewer older contractors who buy through trade channels.

Recommendation: WEP should choose the targeted social media campaign. It reaches the 59% of the 520 contractors who value recycled-composite panels and the 51% who check credentials at low cost, and it scales beyond a single local event. The exhibition is rejected as narrow and costly; trade magazines are rejected as expensive and untargeted. A small exhibition presence can later reinforce the digital message.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of the promotional options with minimal application to WEP.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of WEP with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of WEP with a well-justified recommendation explaining why trade magazines and the exhibition are rejected.

questions.question_text: WEP has a flat organisational structure with laissez-faire leadership, yet faces a shortage of trained machine operators and rising panel waste. Explain two benefits for WEP of this approach in tackling those problems.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Laissez-faire leadership in a flat structure gives WEP's 31 staff freedom to experiment with the new pressing line, so machine operators can adjust settings to cut the 9.1% waste fibre rate without waiting for approval through layers of management. Fast, practical responses protect the $6.00 contribution on each panel and ease the pressure on the $690,000 investment, while the lack of hierarchy helps attract skilled operators who value autonomy.

Point 2: Delegating problem-solving encourages the 12 staff without on-the-job training to learn by working alongside experienced colleagues, building the operator skills WEP lacks and reducing the 2.2% defect rate. Ownership of quality decisions also helps answer the complaints that rose from 22 to 35 per month and protects the 4.1-day delivery record that builders rely on. In a small workforce, this approach uses local knowledge that a distant manager would miss.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to WEP's skills shortage, waste and delivery.

questions.question_text: WEP must train 12 of its 31 staff on the new pressing line. Consider on-the-job training at the plant or off-the-job courses at the college at $820 per employee. Which should WEP choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Coaching on WEP's own pressing line shows the 12 trainees exactly how to reduce the 9.1% waste fibre and the 2.2% defect rate, costs no course fee, and keeps the 18,000 panels per quarter flowing. It suits the flat, delegated culture, as operators learn from one another on the real line. The weaknesses are that trainers lose time, inconsistent habits may spread, and there is no certificate, which may matter to the 51% of contractors checking environmental credentials.

Off-the-job training: The college course at $820 per employee costs $9,840 for all 12 (12 × $820), modest against the $690,000 line, and offers structured teaching plus a recognised qualification supporting WEP's environmental claims. However, 12 of 31 staff are away from the plant, threatening the 4.1-day delivery record, and the generic syllabus may not match WEP's exact pressing equipment, so on-site follow-up would still be required.

Decision: WEP should prioritise on-the-job training with short certified college modules added later. It is cheaper, specific to the panel line and avoids losing output while waste is a live problem; full off-the-job training alone is rejected because taking 12 staff away and spending $9,840 would disrupt the 72,000-unit plan and still leave machine-specific skills to be learned on site.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to WEP.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both training methods in the context of WEP.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both training methods in the context of WEP with a well-justified decision covering cost, disruption and machine relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how WEP's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $186,000 ÷ ($13.50 − $7.50) = $186,000 ÷ $6.00 = 31,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 31,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $13.50 − $7.50 = $6.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $6.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways WEP's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Break-even of 31,000 units against output of 72,000 units gives a margin of safety of 41,000 units (72,000 − 31,000), showing how far builder demand could fall before the panel line fails to cover $186,000 of fixed costs.
2. Contribution of $6.00 a unit allows managers to test the $0.55 premium: if accepted it raises contribution to $6.55, while if not the 31,000-unit threshold still applies, guiding negotiations with the 520 surveyed contractors.
3. The figures set the volume required to meet the $260,000 lease payments and justify the $690,000 investment, informing how much agricultural waste fibre to buy.
4. Unit cost data ($186,000 ÷ 72,000 units + $7.50 = $10.08 a unit) enables quarterly benchmarking, exposing the 9.1% waste and 2.2% defect rate so managers can respond to the 12.1% rise in fibre, resin and transport costs.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 31,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $6.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety of 41,000 units against 72,000-unit output; testing the $0.55 premium against $186,000 fixed costs; lease and $690,000 volume planning; and unit-cost benchmarking at $10.08 to cut waste.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for the accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate WEP's financial performance by calculating the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has performance improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 40.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 45.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 12.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 15.0%
ROCE 2024 = 12.0%
ROCE 2025 = 15.0%

Detailed workings: 2024 gross profit of $320,000 on revenue of $800,000 gives 320 ÷ 800 = 0.400; 2025 gross profit of $432,000 on $960,000 gives 432 ÷ 960 = 0.450. Operating profit of $96,000 ÷ $800,000 = 0.120 and $144,000 ÷ $960,000 = 0.150. Returns on capital employed of $800,000 and $960,000 are 96 ÷ 800 = 0.120 and 144 ÷ 960 = 0.150.

Evaluation: Every measure is higher. The 40.0% to 45.0% rise in the first margin reflects revenue growing by $160,000 while cost of sales increased only $48,000, so the extra recycled-composite panel sales were won with proportionately less material cost. The 12.0% to 15.0% rise in operating profitability shows the $186,000 fixed costs were spread over 72,000 panels, and the 12.0% to 15.0% return on capital shows the new line is earning on a larger asset base. However, interest payable rose from $15,000 to $20,000 as the $260,000 lease took effect, and a 12.1% rise in fibre, resin and transport costs could erode the cost advantage next year. The 9.1% waste fibre rate also indicates further savings are possible.

Conclusion: WEP's performance has improved. Higher revenue, a smaller proportionate rise in cost of sales and stronger operating profit lift both margins and the return on capital. The main threats are lease finance costs and continuing input inflation, which management should monitor, but the 2024–2025 evidence shows a genuine and broad improvement.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the three profitability measures for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of revenue, cost of sales, capital employed and interest movements and a justified conclusion on whether performance improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for WEP of making recycled-composite panels from agricultural waste fibre.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Agricultural waste fibre supports the survey result that 59% of the 520 contractors questioned would pay up to $0.55 more for recycled-composite panels, protecting the $6.00 contribution per unit while fibre, resin and transport costs rise 12.1%. It also appeals to the 51% who check environmental credentials, sustaining the $690,000 line and the 72,000-unit output sold at $13.50.

Disadvantage: Agricultural waste fibre can vary in quality and supply, which may raise the 2.2% defect rate and the 9.1% waste fibre level as the pressing line is adjusted, pushing up the $7.50 variable cost per unit. Collection and treatment of the fibre also add cost, so unless the full $0.55 premium is secured from builders, margins will be squeezed while the shortage of trained machine operators and a 35-per-month complaint level make the first year difficult.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to WEP's survey data, costs and panel quality.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 5.00%, the 6.5% minimum wage increase and the 12.1% rise in recycled fibre, resin and transport costs will affect WEP. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.25% to 5.00%): If the $260,000 lease is linked to the base rate, a 0.75 percentage point increase adds 0.0075 × $260,000 = $1,950 a year. This is small beside fixed costs of $186,000, and the $430,000 retained profit used for the line means WEP has little rate-sensitive debt. The broader worry is that dearer credit could cool the 2.2% growth in commercial building, reducing panel orders.

Minimum wage increase (6.5%, to $13.53 an hour): WEP employs a workforce of 31 at the plant, so wage costs will rise and cannot be avoided. The insert gives no hours worked and no individual pay, so a total wage bill cannot be calculated honestly. The defensible test is productivity: 72,000 units ÷ 31 staff ≈ 2,323 panels per employee, so the rise is bearable only if that output holds and the 2.2% defect rate falls; otherwise unit labour cost eats into the $6.00 contribution.

Fibre, resin and transport costs (12.1%): These go directly into every panel. Since the $7.50 variable cost is not decomposed, only a labelled bound can be shown: if all of it rose 12.1%, that adds 0.121 × $7.50 = $0.91 per unit (rounded); over 72,000 units that is $65,520 a year (72,000 × $0.91). Even a partial rise would cut contribution from $6.00 toward about $5.09, and the $0.55 premium available to 59% of contractors offsets only part of it.

Conclusion: The 12.1% rise in recycled fibre, resin and transport costs will have the greatest impact. It applies to every panel, directly reduces the contribution that covers the $260,000 lease and supports the $690,000 investment, and cannot be removed by a refinancing decision. The interest effect is small and bounded at $1,950, while the wage effect depends on hours not stated and can be offset by productivity, so both are secondary threats.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to WEP.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on WEP's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of WEP with a well-justified judgment that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
